Macquaria ambigua, the Australian golden perch, exhibits a life history closely tied to the thermal regimes of its inland river systems. Spawning is triggered by spring floods and rising water temperatures, with larval development proceeding rapidly under warm conditions. In controlled hatchery settings, the transition from fertilised ovum to yolk-sac larva occurs swiftly; when incubating eggs are maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at birth is a mere 1.3 days [ab = 1.3 days], reflecting the rapid metabolic pace of early ontogeny in this warmwater percichthyid. The resulting larvae are initially lecithotrophic, subsisting on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. This brief embryonic period is an adaptation to the unpredictable flow regimes of Australia's arid-zone rivers, favouring rapid development during ephemeral flood events. Comparative data from related percichthyids suggest that such abbreviated incubation times are typical for species spawning in warm, turbid waters where predation pressure on eggs is high. The ecological cost of this accelerated early development is a small initial size, as the wet weight at birth is only 0.014 grams [Wwb = 0.014 grams], a mass largely comprising the yolk sac that sustains the prolarva through its first days of life.

As the species progresses through the larval-juvenile transition, growth trajectories diverge between the sexes, a pattern common among iteroparous freshwater teleosts. Sexual maturation in females is tied to the attainment of a critical body size rather than a strict chronological age, with energy reserves directing vitellogenesis onset. Field surveys and captive growth studies consistently indicate that the total length at puberty for females is 45 centimeters [Lp = 45 centimeters], a size threshold that is typically reached between three and five years of age depending on local productivity and thermal conditions. This length at first maturation ensures that females have sufficient body cavity volume for ovarian development and that they can produce a clutch of eggs that maximizes offspring survival under variable flow conditions. Mark-recapture data from the Murray-Darling Basin corroborate that females smaller than 45 cm rarely exhibit gravid condition upon capture, confirming this as a reliable indicator of reproductive activation. The concordance between laboratory growth curves and field observations underscores the robustness of this size-based maturation schedule across the species' expansive natural range.

Under sustained thermal conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females at their largest size produce approximately 1,370 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,370 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the high fecundity typical of batch-spawning species adapted to environments where recruitment success is episodic, a formulation derived from observed spawning events recorded over multiple breeding seasons. This daily reproductive output is supported by intensive vitellogenic activity during the protracted spawning season, which in the Murray River can extend from October through February. The species is an asynchronous spawner, releasing multiple batches over the season so that this egg production rate is sustained rather than concentrated into a single event. This strategy buffers against the loss of any single cohort to sudden flow recessions or temperature fluctuations. Hydrographic data suggest that years with extended spring floods correlate with the highest observed total fecundity per female, reinforcing the coupling between thermal stability and reproductive investment in this species.

The ultimate size attained by female Macquaria ambigua in large, productive rivers represents one of the maximum values recorded for any Australian freshwater percichthyid. A total length of 76 centimeters [Li = 76 centimeters] has been documented from commercial catch records in the lower Murray River, and this corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 24,000 grams [Wwi = 24,000 grams] in the largest gravid females. This asymptotic mass and length are achieved after many years of growth, with the growth rate slowing noticeably after the onset of sexual maturation. The relationship between total length and body mass in these large adults follows a near-isometric scaling, indicating that the heaviest individuals maintain robust body condition into advanced age. Comparable records from impoundments suggest that reservoir-dwelling females can reach similar ultimate lengths, though their ultimate weight rarely exceeds 20,000 grams in most lentic environments. The attainment of such large size is energetically expensive and is likely supported by the abundant decapod and teleost prey available in lowland river reaches during high-flow years, a correlation supported by stable isotope analyses from the Darling River system.

Longevity in this species is considerable for an iteroparous freshwater fish inhabiting a variable environment, a trait that allows individuals multiple reproductive opportunities across decades. Under the thermal conditions prevailing in regulated rivers maintained at approximately 23 °C [T = 23 °C] during the growing season, the maximum recorded lifespan is 7,300 days [am = 7,300 days], equivalent to twenty years based on otolith annulus counts from the oldest individuals collected in the Murray River system. This extended lifespan allows a single female to participate in perhaps fifteen or more spawning seasons, given that first reproduction begins around the fifth year. The oldest fish are often the largest, and studies confirm that these senescent individuals still produce viable gametes, although egg size may decline with age. This life-history strategy is contrasted with that of smaller, shorter-lived species in the same community, such as the Murray hardyhead, which complete their life cycle in two to three years. The longevity of Macquaria ambigua at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] is therefore a key demographic trait that stabilizes populations through prolonged reproductive contribution during periods of poor recruitment.
